parts.title: Hold, move and drive a qubit
parts.summary: Learn which object carries the information, which field acts on it, and what a measurement can prove.

lessons.title: What can a machine ask a qubit to do?
lessons.hook: Start with two photographs of the same experiment. By the end you can point to three different jobs in the pictures: holding an atom, changing the information it carries, and finding out what happened.

lessons.title: How do you carry a qubit across a chip?
lessons.hook: Two laboratories need distant partners to meet. Follow the moving trap in each apparatus, identify what stays still, then decide what evidence would show a successful journey.

lessons.title: How does a pulse become a gate?
lessons.hook: A burst can move a qubit all the way from 0 to 1, halfway, or back where it started. Use a swing to reason about frequency, then use two pulses to reason about phase.

lessons.title: How would you know the gate worked?
lessons.hook: A correctly timed voltage is encouraging. To learn what it did to the qubit, use repeated trials, a calibration sweep, and sequences that should return you to a known state.

parts.title: Generate and deliver a signal
parts.summary: Choose a component by its output. Make voltage samples, build a tone, then deliver it to an electrode or a beam.

lessons.title: Turn a number into a voltage
lessons.hook: A computer can store the number 3. An electrode responds to volts. Follow one number across that boundary, then look at a measured output to see how long the change takes.

lessons.title: Keep a wave in phase
lessons.hook: How can a controller produce a steady tone for a million cycles and still know its phase? Build the digital equivalent of a clock hand, then locate it in QubiC.

lessons.title: Play a waveform from memory
lessons.hook: How can a host computer ask for a precisely timed pulse without sending every sample at the instant it is needed? Store the shape first, then give a local player a start command.

lessons.title: Give a fast wave a shape
lessons.hook: A radio can carry slow changes on a rapid oscillation. A qubit drive uses the same idea. Follow the pulse shape through a memory, a mixer and an output cable.

lessons.title: Choose a laser for the job
lessons.hook: A machine can point several colours of light at the same atom. Read the Lukin-group apparatus as a wiring diagram and work out which beam holds the atom and which changes its internal state.

lessons.title: Hold one atom in an optical tweezer
lessons.hook: What keeps an atom inside a spot of light even when no gate is playing? Follow the force across the focus and predict what happens if the focus starts moving.

lessons.title: Steer light with sound
lessons.hook: The atoms need a moving spot of light. Learn what a lens does, why sound can steer a beam, and how a laboratory measures the distance moved per change of frequency.

lessons.title: Shape an electric well with electrodes
lessons.hook: How can stationary pieces of metal carry an ion around a bend? Read the racetrack drawing, then trace the voltage command that shifts a well.

parts.title: Collect and interpret a response
parts.summary: Follow two kinds of evidence back from the apparatus: a returning microwave tone and a stream of photons.

lessons.title: Read a qubit through a resonator
lessons.hook: A cold chip can return information along a cable even while the qubit stays in place. Identify the object that rings, the wave that probes it, and the quantity that comes back.

lessons.title: Sample a returning voltage
lessons.hook: A readout cable brings back a changing voltage. Learn how it becomes a list of numbers and why one number rarely identifies the state of a qubit.

lessons.title: Decide which state produced a signal
lessons.hook: Suppose each trial gives a noisy wave. Compare it with a reference, combine the evidence across samples, and decide where to draw the boundary between two answers.

lessons.title: Count flashes from an ion
lessons.hook: One internal state scatters many photons when illuminated. Learn how a detector turns individual flashes into a count, and why a dark observation is ambiguous.

parts.title: Program the FPGA
parts.summary: Configure a truth table, inspect its transistor switches, capture a bit, and connect working Verilog to physical pins.

lessons.title: Give two events a common clock
lessons.hook: Two boards receive the same program. Will their pulses arrive together? Separate the rate of ticking, the alignment of tick zero, and the time needed to travel down a cable.

lessons.title: Program a circuit with a truth table
lessons.hook: Suppose a cable carries two yes-or-no answers. Build a circuit that signals when exactly one is yes. Then change what the circuit computes by rewriting four bits.

lessons.title: Capture one bit on a clock edge
lessons.hook: A detector result may change while another circuit is reading it. Build one bit of memory, change an input between clock edges, and predict which level reaches the output.

lessons.title: Write, test and load a hardware design
lessons.hook: Write the clocked table as a short circuit description. Test it with artificial pins, then follow the path from named ports to a switch and a light on a real board.

lessons.title: Buffer commands in a queue
lessons.hook: A producer can briefly be faster than a consumer. Build a four-slot queue on paper and decide exactly when an entry appears, moves or waits.

lessons.title: Hand one command to a laboratory board
lessons.hook: The FPGA must receive commands and release them in order. Follow a command from a queue to package pins and then to an instrument connector on the INO experiment controller.

parts.title: Decode and act on errors
parts.summary: Start with two clues about a flip. Work up to the Helios decoder and distinguish a result check from a latency measurement.

lessons.title: Decode two clues about three qubits
lessons.hook: You have three stored bits and permission to ask whether neighbours agree. Use just those two clues to locate one flip, then see why real decoders need a model of what can go wrong.

lessons.title: How a decoder grows across a chip
lessons.hook: An error can leave clues separated in space or time. Follow the work of matching those clues, then compare two implementations of the Helios algorithm.

lessons.title: Step inside a Helios decoder link
lessons.hook: Open a circuit taken directly from the Helios hardware design. Watch two neighbouring workers grow a shared edge, then find the clock cycle when its status becomes visible.

parts.title: Replay published machines
parts.summary: Trace native IBM pulse schedules, a Harvard–MIT moving pair and Quantinuum’s 32-ion phase scan. Each case names its evidence and reconstruction.

lessons.title: IBM Quantum Manila · read a native pulse schedule
lessons.hook: Read an IBM pulse schedule from the first rotation to the grouped measurement on five qubits.

lessons.title: Lukin group · carry an entangled pair
lessons.hook: Replay the transport interval from Bluvstein and colleagues’ 2022 experiment. Watch two atoms separate while a second set of laser pulses protects their phase, then read the evidence that the state survived.

lessons.title: Quantinuum H2 · follow the 32-ion phase scan
lessons.hook: Start with the first interacting pair in a published 32-ion circuit. Follow the pair into a gate zone, then ask why the experiment ends with 32 measurements at each of many different phases.

parts.title: What you are looking at
parts.summary: A quantum computer is a stack: a program, timed hardware operations, firmware for control processors, wires, and the qubits at the end. Learn to read every layer of one run.

lessons.title: The stack in one picture
lessons.hook: A three-line program becomes 400 events on 24 parts. Follow it from the source line to the qubit.

lessons.title: Batches: the clock everything runs on
lessons.hook: Every time in the machine is a whole number of clock cycles. Find out how long one is, and why.

lessons.title: Following one pulse
lessons.hook: One store instruction, one link, one queue, one DAC, one coax, one qubit. Walk the causal chain.

lessons.title: Reading the workspace
lessons.hook: Four synchronized layers and a 3D stage. Learn which question each one answers.

parts.title: Programming the controller
parts.summary: The control processor does not play pulses; it schedules them ahead of time through memory-mapped registers. Learn the mechanism that makes timing exact.

lessons.title: Posted writes and the pulse table
lessons.hook: A pulse is a row in a table. Firing it is one store to one address.

lessons.title: Timed queues and the lead
lessons.hook: Issue early, land exactly. Why the firmware works 96 cycles in the future.

lessons.title: Measurement results come back
lessons.hook: A demodulation window, a decoder pipeline and a load that stalls until the bit is ready.

lessons.title: Cores meet: the board hub
lessons.hook: Shared bits, barriers and mailboxes, one message per cycle for the whole board.

parts.title: Three machines, one controller
parts.summary: Superconducting qubits, trapped ions and neutral atoms differ in physics but share one control problem. See how the same controller drives each.

lessons.title: Superconducting: from OpenQASM to microwaves
lessons.hook: Gates become calibrated microwave pulses, virtual Z becomes a phase, and readout is a tone plus a window.

lessons.title: Trapped ions: shuttling is a waveform
lessons.hook: An ion moves because electrode voltages change. Every hop is a burst of DAC waveforms.

lessons.title: Neutral atoms: tones carry atoms
lessons.hook: An acousto-optic deflector turns an RF frequency into a position. Step the frequency and the atom follows.

lessons.title: The same controller everywhere
lessons.hook: Compare the three runs: what changes, what stays, and what limits each.

parts.title: Designing hardware
parts.summary: A machine is a document: parts, positions, channels and routed wires, checked against rules. Change the hardware and watch the timing change.

lessons.title: A machine is a document
lessons.hook: Parts, channels, wires and calibrations: read the design of an eight-qubit ring.

lessons.title: Wire length is latency
lessons.hook: Move the chip two metres away and every pulse arrives 10 ns later. Nothing at the converters changes.

lessons.title: Who drives what
lessons.hook: Give three qubits to one core and the feed-forward never touches the hub.

lessons.title: When a design breaks a rule
lessons.hook: Converters of the wrong kind, wires that end nowhere, readouts that return too late.

parts.title: Fault tolerance on the controller
parts.summary: Error correction needs measurements, decoding and corrections within a deadline. Measure what the control system costs, and run a real decoder on a control core.

lessons.title: Feedback latency
lessons.hook: From the end of a readout window to the conditioned pulse: every nanosecond accounted for.

lessons.title: System calls
lessons.hook: measure, decode_syndrome, pauli_frame_update: a fault-tolerant program as calls on the controller.

lessons.title: A real decoder on a control core
lessons.hook: The C union-find of the Helios decoder, compiled for RISC-V and checked against its own test vectors.

lessons.title: Limits: bandwidth, concurrency, depth
lessons.hook: How many bits per microsecond, how many pulses at once, how deep a link. Find where a schedule stops fitting.

background.title: Qubits and what controls them
background.summary: Transmons, trapped ions and neutral atoms: what a qubit is in each, and which signals act on it.

background.title: Classical control systems
background.summary: FPGAs, DACs, ADCs, numerically controlled oscillators, clocks, cables and optics.

background.title: The RISC-Q architecture
background.summary: One RISC-V core per channel group, posted writes, pulse tables, timed queues, sinks and the board hub.

background.title: Deterministic timing
background.summary: Why control systems schedule ahead, what the lead covers, and what the Lean proofs guarantee.

background.title: Measurement, feedback and decoding
background.summary: Readout, feed-forward, syndromes, decoders and the deadline every error-correction round must meet.

background.title: How this simulator works
background.summary: Lowering, firmware, the Lean model, the trace, and what is proved, tested or assumed.

background.title: Numbers and sources
background.summary: Every latency, duration and rate the simulator uses, with where it comes from.

background.title: Glossary
background.summary: Every term of the course, in one sentence each.
